cards.front: In Rh(D)-negative women, Anti-D is indicated for vaginal bleeding at or after [___] weeks gestation or for any miscarriage requiring surgical/medical intervention; it is not routinely needed for a threatened miscarriage before that threshold.
cards.context:
Sensitising events in early pregnancy: any vaginal bleeding ≥12 weeks, miscarriage requiring intervention (medical/surgical), TOP, ectopic, molar, CVS, abdominal trauma.

Exception: threatened miscarriage <12 weeks generally doesn't need anti-D — low risk of significant fetomaternal haemorrhage at this gestation.

The T1 dose is 250 IU IM (smaller than the 625 IU for T2/T3 events) reflecting smaller fetal blood volume. Only Rh(D)-negative women need anti-D.

cards.front: At 19 weeks, monochorionic diamniotic twins have fluid pockets of 9 cm and 1 cm. The donor bladder remains unseen throughout the scan; Dopplers are normal, and neither twin has hydrops. The Quintero classification is [___].
cards.context:
Fluid discordance establishes the syndrome; loss of the donor bladder moves it beyond stage I.

Normal Dopplers and no hydrops exclude stages III and IV. Staging describes findings, not an inevitable stepwise sequence.

cards.front: Anticoagulant of choice throughout pregnancy is [___]; warfarin is teratogenic at 6-12 weeks; DOACs are contraindicated.
cards.context:
LMWH does not cross the placenta, so it is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy. After birth, LMWH or warfarin is compatible with breastfeeding.

Warfarin crosses the placenta and is most teratogenic at 6-12 weeks; later exposure risks fetal intracranial bleeding.

Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) lack pregnancy safety data and are contraindicated. Use indication- and weight-appropriate LMWH dosing under the relevant protocol.

cards.front: PALM-COEIN groups abnormal uterine bleeding causes by mechanism. The PALM half lists four anatomic lesions: polyp, adenomyosis, [___], and malignancy/hyperplasia. For heavy bleeding without an anatomic cause, the first-line treatment is the LNG-IUS.
cards.context:
PALM-COEIN (FIGO) splits AUB causes by anatomy: PALM = anatomic lesions (polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy); COEIN = non-anatomic (coagulopathy, ovulatory, endometrial, iatrogenic, not-yet-classified).

Anatomy drives workup. PALM needs pelvic USS or MRI plus endometrial biopsy if age >45 or risk factors.

First-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding without anatomic cause is the levonorgestrel IUS (Mirena) — 90% bleeding reduction at 12 months.

cards.front: In NSW, termination of pregnancy is available on request up to 22 weeks; beyond that requires [___] practitioners and a hospital setting.
cards.context:
The 22-week threshold in NSW (and most Australian states) reflects fetal viability and aligns with the legal framework when termination was decriminalised.

State-by-state variation: VIC allows on-request abortion to 24 weeks; QLD + SA cluster around 22 weeks.

 Since March 2024, WA allows abortion on request to 23 weeks; after 23 weeks two practitioners are required, and the former Ministerial Panel approval process has been abolished. Check current local legislation.

cards.front: Because mesh exposure offsets its benefit, a first anterior prolapse repair uses [___].
cards.context:
Fewer returning bulges are not a free win. The same mesh that holds the anterior wall can come through the vagina, and the combined return-to-theatre rate is higher.

That trade-off is why a first repair stays with native tissue. Mesh is not forbidden forever, but it is not the opening operation.

cards.front: The 4 Ts of PPH causes: Tone (atony, ~70%), [___] (lacerations, ~20%), Tissue (retained, ~10%), and Thrombin.
cards.context:
4 Ts mnemonic ranks PPH causes by frequency: Tone (atony, ~70% — uterus fails to contract); Trauma (~20% — perineal/vaginal/cervical lacerations); Tissue (~10% — retained placenta or products)

Thrombin (~1% — coagulopathy). PPH = ≥500 mL after vaginal delivery or ≥1000 mL after CS. Surgical: B-Lynch, uterine artery ligation/embolisation, hysterectomy as last resort.

cards.front: Group B streptococcus (GBS)-positive women receive intrapartum IV [___] in labour to prevent neonatal sepsis; ideally given at least 4 hours before delivery.
cards.context:
GBS colonises the lower genital tract in 20-30% of women asymptomatically; vertical transmission during birth → early-onset neonatal GBS disease (sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis) in the first week.

Intrapartum IV benzylpenicillin (3 g load, then 1.8 g every 4 h until delivery) prevents this. Routine vaginal-rectal GBS swab at 35-37 weeks; positive → intrapartum antibiotics.

If GBS status unknown in labour, treat empirically if: preterm <37 weeks, ROM ≥18 h, intrapartum fever ≥38°C, previous GBS baby, or GBS bacteriuria.

cards.front: ECV is offered from [___] weeks for breech presentation; success rate is approximately 50%.
cards.context:
ECV = manual rotation of breech baby to cephalic by abdominal manipulation, done at 36-37 weeks (earlier baby may turn back; later uterus too tight + fluid too low).

Success ~50% overall, ~70% with multiparity/posterior placenta/adequate liquor/non-engaged breech/operator experience. Contraindications: placenta praevia, APH, ruptured membranes, abnormal CTG, multiple pregnancy.

Tocolysis (terbutaline 250 µg subcut) improves success; monitor CTG before/during/30-60 min after; if ECV fails → planned CS at 39 weeks.

cards.front: Ovulation can return as early as [___] days postpartum in non-breastfeeding women, so contraception must be discussed before discharge — not deferred to the 6-week check.
cards.context:
The 21-day rule applies to non-breastfeeding women — ovulation can return this early, well before menses, so the next pregnancy can begin without warning.

In breastfeeding women, LAM provides ~98% effective contraception only when ALL three criteria are met: exclusively breastfeeding (no supplements, gaps <6h overnight/<4h daytime), amenorrhoeic, baby <6 months.

cards.front: EPDS interpretation thresholds: a total score of [___] is the cut-off for probable depression (full psychiatric assessment); scores of 10-12 are possible cases (repeat in 2-4 weeks); a positive response on the dedicated self-harm item triggers immediate safety assessment regardless of total score.
cards.context:
EPDS is a 10-item self-report questionnaire (scored 0-30) validated for antenatal + postnatal screening.

Interpretation: <10 = low risk, routine follow-up; 10-12 = possible, repeat in 2-4 weeks; ≥13 = probable, full psychiatric assessment.

cards.front: MgSO₄ for fetal neuroprotection is given when imminent birth is anticipated before 30 weeks: [___] g IV loading dose, then 1 g/h infusion until birth or 24 h. The number-needed-to-treat to prevent one case of cerebral palsy is approximately 63.
cards.context:
MgSO₄ given antenatally for imminent preterm birth <30 weeks reduces cerebral palsy in survivors by ~30% (Cochrane). Mechanism is uncertain — possibly preventing glutamate excitotoxicity in the immature brain.

Regimen: 4 g IV loading over 20-30 min, then 1 g/h infusion for ≥4 h before delivery — aim as close to 4 h before birth as possible.

NNT ≈63: treat ~63 mothers to prevent one case of cerebral palsy. A modest absolute benefit, but cheap and low-risk, so given routinely at this gestation.

cards.front: PPROM (preterm prelabour rupture of membranes) diagnosis: history of fluid gush + [___] examination showing pooling of amniotic fluid; avoid digital vaginal exam (raises infection risk, shortens latency).
cards.context:
The 'no digital VE in PPROM' rule is a key safety rule: each digital exam introduces vaginal flora into the cervix and through ruptured membranes, raising chorioamnionitis risk + shortening latency by hours.

Use sterile speculum instead — visualises cervix + pooling without entering the os. If labour established and you need dilatation, a single careful digital exam may be unavoidable — document the indication.

'Gush' history is sensitive but not specific (urinary incontinence, discharge, amniocentesis leak can mimic) — confirm with speculum + IGFBP-1/PAMG-1 if uncertain.

cards.front: The PITCHES trial (2019) showed ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) does not reduce adverse perinatal outcomes in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP); the most important intervention is [___] timing based on bile acid level.
cards.context:
UDCA was the standard ICP treatment for decades on observational evidence.

UDCA remains widely used for symptomatic relief but focus shifted to delivery timing as the single most outcome-influencing intervention.

Weekly bile acid monitoring catches escalating disease.

cards.front: A T-piece device needs working [___], so a self-inflating bag is kept beside it if that delivery fails.
cards.context:
The T-piece is suggested because pressure and oxygen can be set and watched. Those breaths stop if the wall gas or the hose fails.

A flow-inflating bag has the same weakness. The self-inflating bag still refills from the room, which is why it stays on the cot.

cards.front: After an abnormal auscultation, a cardiotocograph is normal, with no maternal or fetal risk factors and a reassuring clinical assessment. Consider returning to [___].
cards.context:
If cardiotocography is normal after an abnormal auscultation finding and no maternal or fetal risk factors remain, intermittent auscultation may be resumed.

The woman's overall risk and the reason for the original concern still guide the decision.

cards.front: Empirical antibiotics for early-onset neonatal sepsis: [___] (covers GBS) + gentamicin (covers Gram-negatives like E. coli); stop at 36-48 hours if cultures negative + well.
cards.context:
EONS (<72 h) is dominated by vertically transmitted maternal flora — GBS and E. coli account for ~70%.

Empirical antibiotics target both: benzylpenicillin (GBS, Listeria, syphilis) + gentamicin (E. coli and other Gram-negatives, synergistic with penicillin against GBS); doses benzylpen 60 mg/kg IV 12-hourly.

LONS (>72 h) more often nosocomial — flucloxacillin (Staph) + gent. Add aciclovir 20 mg/kg IV 8-hourly if HSV suspected (vesicles, focal neurology, maternal active genital herpes).

cards.front: Preconception [___] supplementation reduces the risk of fetal neural tube defects.
cards.context:
The classic preconception intervention: start BEFORE conception and continue through the first trimester, when the neural tube closes.

High-dose is used for higher-risk women (previous NTD, diabetes, certain medications).

cards.front: The first manoeuvre for shoulder dystocia is the [___] manoeuvre (hyperflexing the maternal hips).
cards.context:
Shoulder dystocia is a 'no traction' emergency.

The first and often sufficient manoeuvre is McRoberts (hyperflex maternal hips onto the abdomen) plus suprapubic pressure — it rotates the pelvis to free the anterior shoulder.

cards.front: Vitamin K prophylaxis: preferred [___] dose 1 mg at birth; if declined, oral regimen is three doses over 4 weeks.
cards.context:
VKDB (formerly HDN) affects neonates because the liver doesn't synthesise factors II, VII, IX, X without vitamin K, and breast milk has minimal vitamin K.

IM vitamin K 1 mg at birth — single-dose, near-100% effective, no compliance issues.

cards.front: Initial intrauterine resuscitation for prolonged fetal bradycardia: maternal repositioning and stop uterotonics; if persistent, proceed to category 1 [___].
cards.context:
Prolonged fetal bradycardia (FHR <110 for >3 min) is a peripartum emergency. If unresolved by 9 min or with an abnormal CTG, proceed to category 1 caesarean.

Caesarean urgency (RANZCOG): Cat 1 = immediate threat to mother/fetus, deliver ≤30 min; Cat 2 = compromise without immediate threat, ≤75 min; Cat 3 = early delivery, no compromise; Cat 4 = elective.
